name: Smile practice / smile maxxing

lead: Smile maxxing means practising and refining your smile, usually in a mirror, so it looks more natural, symmetrical and warm.

The chain: rehearse the smile, get a more genuine and even expression, and your face reads as warmer and more approachable. Research distinguishes the Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eyes, from the voluntary 'Pan Am' smile using only the mouth, and studies report smiling makes people seem more likable. Smile training itself has not been studied.

paras: People practise in a mirror or on camera, aiming to use the muscles around the eyes as well as the mouth, and check which side and amount of teeth look best. It is a free daily habit often paired with teeth whitening or orthodontics. Facial feedback research suggests expressions may slightly affect mood; a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small effects.
No medical risks reported. Cultural context affects how smiles are read.

chain: Face looks warmer and more attractive
angle.text: Users rehearse their smile in a mirror so it looks more genuine and symmetrical, drawing on the difference between polite and genuine smiles. Studies show smiles make people seem more likable; smile training itself has not been studied.

lead: Smile practice, or smile maxxing, is the practice of training one's smile, often in a mirror, to look more natural, symmetrical or attractive. The goal is a warmer, more approachable and more appealing expression: practitioners work on engaging the eyes as well as the mouth, on how high and wide the smile goes, and on the difference between a polite and a genuine smile. Community discussion focuses on how smiling is perceived.[1]

Research distinguishes the Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eyes (orbicularis oculi) and the cheek-raising zygomatic major, from the voluntary 'Pan Am' smile using only the zygomatic major.[1] Studies reported on Wikipedia say smiling can make people seem more likable and approachable, though perceptions differ across cultures.[1] The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that expressions also influence emotion; a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small but robust effects.[2]
infobox: Zygomatic major; orbicularis oculi for Duchenne smiles[1]

paras: Practice is usually done in front of a mirror or camera, with attention to raising the cheeks, engaging the eye muscles and keeping the smile symmetrical. The smile involves mainly the zygomatic major, and cheek dimples come from a split zygomaticus major whose fibres attach to the skin.[1]

Guillaume Duchenne described the smile type later named after him in his 1862 work on the mechanism of facial expression. The Duchenne smile raises the mouth corners and the cheeks via the orbicularis oculi, and was reported by Messinger, Fogel and Dickson (2001) to be more uniquely associated with positive emotion.[1] Long-term Botox use around the eyes may prevent Duchenne smiles.[1]

Smiling tends to make people seem more likable and approachable.[1] Krys and colleagues (2016) found that in some cultures a smiling person may be judged as less intelligent, and that trust in smiling people was lower in societies with high corruption.[1] Smiling is more common in the US and France than in China or Japan, according to Tsai and colleagues (2016) and Talhelm and colleagues (2019).[1]

Strack, Martin and Stepper (1988) reported that holding a pen between the teeth made cartoons seem funnier. A 17-lab replication led by Wagenmakers (2016) found no systematic effect, a later study attributed the difference to a camera, and Coles, Larsen and Lench (2019) found small effects overall (d about 0.2).[2]
No studies found on smile practice or smile training as a looksmaxxing method. Related research on facial feedback and smile perception is described above.[1][2]

timeline.event: Duchenne describes two types of smile.[1]
